chunks: "By 3D chips I mean ICs where active silicon is stacked vertically, instead of everything sitting on one flat die.
You thin the dies, drill through-silicon vias or use hybrid bonding, and connect the layers directly so signals travel tens of microns up instead of centimetres sideways.

A vertical connection is a few tens of microns, while crossing a die is around a centimetre, so you get far lower delay and energy per bit and you can put thousands of connections in a square millimetre.
That's how HBM works, with DRAM dies stacked on a base die and a very wide interface, and how some CPUs put a big cache die on top of the compute die.
It also saves footprint, which matters in phones. The downsides are mostly heat and cost.
The die at the bottom has to push its heat through the dies above it, or you put the hot die on top near the heat sink.
Power delivery to each layer is harder, you need known-good-die testing before you stack, and if you stack three dies and one is bad you lose the lot.
I'd also mention that people say '3D' for other things like 3D NAND, which is memory cells built vertically on one die, and 3D transistors like FinFETs, which is a different idea."
